l_leucine.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. A meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found leucine alone had no effect on lean mass, handgrip or leg press in older adults (PMID 35845777). Free leucine added nothing to resistance training in young men (PMID 32079916), frail older women (PMID 40926079) or midlife women (PMID 31577520). Two small trials are positive: walking time in institutionalized older adults on 6 g/day (PMID 32230954) and fat-free mass during energy restriction on 3 g/day (PMID 37923932). An umbrella review favors leucine for muscle mass in sarcopenia without saying in its abstract whether that is free leucine (PMID 32483625), and a 2025 meta-analysis calls its evidence low quality and limited when leucine is used alone (PMID 40805998). The stored trials tested an amino acid mixture (PMID 16507602) and a whey drink (PMID 24284442), measuring protein synthesis over hours. The evidence conflicts with no clear benefit for the free leucine on these labels. PMID 35845777 states: 'Leucine-isolated supplementation did not improve muscle mass and strength in elderly.' These sources do not establish a universal standalone 2-3 g clinical threshold or general-population efficacy without the studied preparation and population context. Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

studies.quote: Leucine-isolated supplementation did not improve muscle mass and strength in elderly.

studies.primary_endpoint: not named; leg-press 1RM and muscle cross-sectional area
studies.quote: High-dose leucine supplementation did not enhance gains in muscle strength and mass after a 12-wk RT program in young resistance-trained males consuming adequate amounts of dietary protein.
Leucine had no added anabolic benefit.

studies.quote: The use of l-leucine supplementation can have some beneficial effects on sarcopenia and could be considered for the treatment of sarcopenia in older individuals.

lecithin.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. A Cochrane review of twelve randomized trials reports no clear clinical benefit of lecithin in Alzheimer's or Parkinsonian dementia, though one trial in subjective memory problems favored it (12917896). A double-blind trial of 20 g/day soya bean lecithin in 20 hyperlipidaemic men found no independent effect on serum lipoproteins (9683394), and an exploratory trial of five emulsifiers including soy lecithin found no cholesterol difference from placebo (40816342). The evidence conflicts, with no clear benefit: a 500 mg/day capsule trial reports total and LDL cholesterol falls of 40% to 56% from baseline, not a between-group effect (21490917); 20 g/day raised the HDL/LDL ratio from baseline with no difference in flow-mediated dilation (17006376); 1200 mg/day improved vigor and two cardiovascular measures while a fatigue scale was unchanged (29310653); a lecithin fluid missed its main target measure and improved a secondary responder measure (15662899); and soybean lecithin 10 g three times a day was reported effective in acute cerebral infarction in a study that doesn't state randomization (16200721). No trial of sunflower lecithin was found. PMID 12917896 states: 'Evidence from randomized trials does not support the use of lecithin in the treatment of patients with dementia.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

studies.primary_endpoint: clinical benefit in dementia or cognitive impairment
studies.quote: No trials reported any clear clinical benefit of lecithin for Alzheimer's disease or Parkinsonian dementia.

studies.primary_endpoint: not named; serum lipoprotein, plasma fibrinogen and macromolecular protein complex
studies.quote: Lecithin treatment had no independent effects on serum lipoprotein, plasma fibrinogen or MPC levels in hyperlipidaemic men.

siberian_ginseng.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Evidence on Eleutherococcus senticosus conflicts and shows no clear benefit. A randomized placebo-controlled trial in 96 adults with chronic fatigue reported that overall efficacy was not demonstrated (PMID 14971626). A trial in 20 distance runners reported that the data do not support an ergogenic effect (PMID 8778554), and a crossover in 9 cyclists found no difference in substrate use or 10-km time (PMID 11099371). A 144-person stress trial described any effect of adding it to stress training as negligible (PMID 23740477). One crossover in 9 recreationally trained men reported 23% longer endurance time at 800 mg/day (PMID 21793317). A 20-person trial in older adults found higher social functioning at 4 weeks that did not persist at 8 weeks (PMID 15207399). A 28-person trial reported surrogate autonomic changes (PMID 38525193), and a crossover in 50 women reported less lower-limb edema hours after powder (PMID 27333960). The fatigue and 800 and 1,200 mg trial abstracts do not state whether powder or extract was tested, so this reads the plant across preparations and doesn't say a powder failed. PMID 14971626 states: 'Overall efficacy was not demonstrated.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

cayenne_pepper.applicability_decision: Finished review with no qualifying study for these labels, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Labels print cayenne at 450 to 500 mg or an extract, or give no amount, and no row shows a capsaicinoid amount. The one trial read at that form and amount gave 11 men a single 500 mg dose with 1.25 mg capsaicin (PMID 24267043). Pooled capsaicin trials report a weight difference of 0.51 kg without separating whole cayenne or extract (PMID 36938807). A pooled single-meal result suggests at least 2 mg capsaicinoids taken before a meal (PMID 24246368), an exposure these labels do not print. Gut symptom trials used red pepper powder at 2.5 g/day (PMID 12030948) and enteric-coated pills (PMID 21573941). No study read tested these labels' preparation with a named primary outcome. Abstracts read; full texts not opened, so this does not say the preparation was tested and failed. PMID 24267043 states: 'These results suggest that acute ingestion of 500 mg of cayenne (1.25 mg capsaicin) or evodiamine is not effective at inducing thermogenesis and increasing fat oxidation at rest or during exercise in men.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

quotes.quote: These results suggest that acute ingestion of 500 mg of cayenne (1.25 mg capsaicin) or evodiamine is not effective at inducing thermogenesis and increasing fat oxidation at rest or during exercise in men.

gotu_kola.applicability_decision: Finished review with no qualifying study for these labels, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Labels print herb powder, whole herb extract, or leaf or aerial extract, and none prints the total triterpenic fraction. The stored venous result tested that fraction in a single-blind trial (PMID 11666126), and a review of venous trials says its conclusion needs caution (PMID 23533507). A cognition meta-analysis reports no significant difference from placebo across domains (PMID 28878245). A diabetes trial found no adjusted difference in its primary outcome, HbA1c (PMID 41383475), and an add-on trial found no additional cognitive effect (PMID 36420467). Extract trials reporting working memory (PMID 18191355) and chair stand (PMID 19880441) results name no primary outcome in their abstracts. A macular pigment trial tested a named extract, CA-HE50, that these labels do not print (PMID 41901080). Abstracts read; full texts not opened, so this does not say the preparation was tested and failed. PMID 28878245 states: 'In conclusion, there is not strong evidence to support the use of C. asiatica for cognitive function improvement in each cognitive domain.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

quotes.quote: In conclusion, there is not strong evidence to support the use of C. asiatica for cognitive function improvement in each cognitive domain.

feverfew.applicability_decision: Finished review with no qualifying study for these labels, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Labels print flower, leaf or unspecified feverfew extract, or herb or powder, and none prints MIG-99. The one positive primary result read tested MIG-99, a CO2 extract: 1.9 against 1.3 fewer attacks per month on placebo (PMID 16232154). The dose study of the same extract states it failed to show a significant effect in general (PMID 12230594). A crossover of a dried alcoholic extract found the same number of attacks in both groups (PMID 23195074). The stored 1988 crossover gave dried leaf with no amount in its abstract (PMID 2899663). A 2025 meta-analysis reports a reduction with limits from bias and does not split results by preparation in its abstract (PMID 41422534). Abstracts read; full texts not opened, so this does not say the preparation was tested and failed. The Cochrane review, PMID 25892430, states: 'However, this constitutes low quality evidence, which needs to be confirmed in larger rigorous trials with stable feverfew extracts and clearly defined migraine populations before firm conclusions can be drawn.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

quotes.quote: However, this constitutes low quality evidence, which needs to be confirmed in larger rigorous trials with stable feverfew extracts and clearly defined migraine populations before firm conclusions can be drawn.
MIG-99 failed to show a significant migraine prophylactic effect in general.

d_ribose.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Controlled exercise trials are mostly null (PMIDs 11641371, 12660407, 12580655, 16937963), and in rowers dextrose improved 2,000 m time more than ribose (PMID 16377979). Cardiac results are positive in patients at much higher amounts than the 1.4 to 5.1 g these labels print per serving: a phase 2 trial in 216 patients with heart failure at 15 g/day (PMID 35644694), a crossover in 15 patients with heart failure (PMID 14607200), and 60 g/day for 3 days in 20 men with coronary disease (PMID 1354276). The stored study has no control group (PMID 17109576). PMID 12660407 states: 'Results indicate that oral ribose supplementation (10 g/d for 5 d) does not affect anaerobic exercise capacity or metabolic markers in trained subjects as evaluated in this study.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.
